name: Bone Brown
lede: Bone brown is a dull dark brown pigment made from partly burned bone, now obsolete, which also left its name on a modern greyish-brown.

sections.title: A partly charred bone
sections.body:
Paterson defines bone brown as charred bone dust, set next to the better-known bone black, an ancient pigment from carbonized bones that is still used [1]. The pigment compendium describes bone brown as derived from partially charred bones, black-brown in tone [2]. It adds that Heaton in 1928 listed it as obsolete or of little importance [2].



In the nineteenth century it served as a modifier in compounded colors [2]. Winsor and Newton's 1896 catalogue gave sap green in oil as quercitron lake, ultramarine and bone brown [2]. Olive lake was likewise a blend of quercitron lake and bone brown with ultramarine [2]. The same compendium gives the fuller history of [[sap-green]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The name is first recorded in our sources in 1912, in Ridgway, and again in Maerz and Paul and ISCC-NBS [3]. The swatch #594E45 is a dark, slightly grey brown [3]. It appears in 2,174 of 23,781 paintings, 9.14%, more common than 93% of named colors, as photographed [3]. Vilhelm Hammershøi uses it most, in 21 of 50 works here [3]. The earliest archive match is far older than the name, so that is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of the pigment [3].
